accepted.before: Research in games and virtual collaboration makes self-similar voice worth investigating, with evidence of selected favorable outcomes alongside uncomfortable reactions~\cite{kao2021selfsimilar,guo2024doppelganger}.

accepted.reason: The original wording implied both cited studies found uncomfortable reactions; only Guo et al. report eeriness. This keeps the first-page tension in accurate form and drops the vague 'selected favorable outcomes', which the next subsection states precisely.
accepted.claude_after: Research in games and virtual collaboration makes self-similar voice worth investigating, although resemblance has also been rated as eerie~\cite{kao2021selfsimilar,guo2024doppelganger}.

accepted.before: The selected work leaves the present comparison unresolved: what changes when the voice guiding an initially unnamed, surrounding object-search task resembles its listener rather than being a preferred catalog choice? The design combines a consequential use for speech with a comparator that already accommodates preference. Its contribution will be to establish how those two voice configurations differ in this setting, including outcomes that favor neither configuration consistently.
accepted.after: The selected work does not address this comparison when the voice guides an initially unnamed target through a surrounding object search. The design combines a consequential use for speech with a comparator that already accommodates preference. Its contribution will be to estimate whether and how those two voice configurations differ in this setting, including outcomes that favor neither configuration consistently.
accepted.reason: Removes a second rhetorical question that repeats the paragraph above. 'Establish how they differ' assumed a difference exists; 'estimate whether and how' fits the two-sided RQ1.
accepted.claude_after: The selected work does not address this comparison when the voice guides an initially unnamed target through a surrounding object search. The design combines a consequential use for speech with a comparator that already accommodates preference. Its contribution will be to estimate whether and how those two voice configurations differ in this setting, including outcomes that favor neither configuration consistently.

accepted.after: Jev, the cloud decision agent shared by both voice conditions, selects from a constrained set of options rather than generating free-form instructions.

accepted.claude_after: Jev, the cloud decision agent shared by both voice conditions, selects from a constrained set of options rather than generating free-form instructions.

accepted.before: The experiment does not vary Jev, memory, or gaze-awareness as independent factors, and the condition contrast cannot isolate acoustic resemblance from every other property of the selected and synthesized voices.
accepted.after: The experiment does not vary Jev, memory, or gaze-awareness as independent factors.

accepted.claude_after: The experiment does not vary Jev, memory, or gaze-awareness as independent factors.

accepted.before: Controller pointing is a distinct input observation, but its spoken acknowledgment is not independent of gaze, because the admission rule also requires valid nearby gaze. accepted.after: Controller pointing is a distinct input observation, but its spoken acknowledgment is not independent of gaze: the documented rule requires a qualified one-second controller hold with valid gaze in the target vicinity when speech is admitted.

accepted.before: Guidance diagnostics establish exposure and technical context, so the statistical comparison concerns voice configuration rather than the independent value of Jev or gaze contingency.
accepted.after: Guidance diagnostics describe exposure and technical context. Because Jev and gaze contingency are shared by both conditions, the statistical comparison concerns voice configuration rather than their independent value.

accepted.claude_after: Guidance diagnostics describe exposure and technical context. Because Jev and gaze contingency are shared by both conditions, the statistical comparison concerns voice configuration rather than their independent value.

accepted.before: It will not automatically adjust away behavior-dependent hint counts or waiting time: these can occur during the task and are not interchangeable with baseline difficulty, as discussed in Chapter~\ref{ch:analysis}.
accepted.after: It will not automatically adjust away behavior-dependent hint counts or waiting time: these arise after voice assignment, may themselves depend on voice condition, and are not interchangeable with baseline difficulty, as discussed in Chapter~\ref{ch:analysis}.
accepted.reason: 'Can occur during the task' gave a weak reason. The actual reason in Chapter 6 is that these behaviors come after assignment and may be caused by the voice condition.
accepted.claude_after: It will not automatically adjust away behavior-dependent hint counts or waiting time: these arise after voice assignment, may themselves depend on voice condition, and are not interchangeable with baseline difficulty, as discussed in Chapter~\ref{ch:analysis}.

accepted.before: A difference accompanied by systematic intelligibility problems in the catalog condition would not isolate resemblance cleanly. accepted.after: A difference accompanied by systematic intelligibility or delivery problems in the catalog condition could reflect those problems rather than anything specific to self-similarity. If both conditions have comparable delivery quality and participants recognize the clone, the result would more directly support a voice-condition effect in this task, although it would still not separate resemblance from other differences between the chosen and synthesized voices.
accepted.reason: The original implied that, apart from delivery faults, the design could isolate resemblance, which contradicts the caveats in Chapters 1 and 4. The non-isolation boundary is now restated at the point where a favorable result would be read.
accepted.claude_after: A difference accompanied by systematic intelligibility or delivery problems in the catalog condition could reflect those problems rather than anything specific to self-similarity. If both conditions have comparable delivery quality and participants recognize the clone, the result would more directly support a voice-condition effect in this task, although it would still not separate resemblance from other differences between the chosen and synthesized voices.

accepted.after: If the preferred catalog voice produces faster completion, that would be consistent with a selected external voice being easier to follow, or with intelligibility or delivery problems in the cloned condition; delivery records and acoustic-quality reporting could help distinguish these readings, but the study would not establish the mechanism without further evidence.
accepted.reason: Applies the delivery-quality caveat to both voices. Before, only the catalog voice's problems were considered. Only measures already planned in Chapters 1 and 5 are mentioned.
accepted.claude_after: If the preferred catalog voice produces faster completion, that would be consistent with a selected external voice being easier to follow, or with intelligibility or delivery problems in the cloned condition; delivery records and acoustic-quality reporting could help distinguish these readings, but the study would not establish the mechanism without further evidence.

remaining_issues: Chapters 4 and 5 define the same measures twice: the T_active formula, starting theta and height difference, head-motion accumulation, contact latencies and instruction counts. Chapter 4 should state the operational definitions and point to Chapter 5 for rationale and edge cases, or the reverse. This is a structural cut, too large for exact-string edits.

Chapter 6 reads like two drafts joined together. 'Primary contrast', 'Secondary and exploratory outcomes', 'Incomplete and interrupted observations' and 'Guidance and qualitative evaluation' are covered again in 'A Candidate Primary Model', 'Secondary Outcomes and Multiplicity', 'Data Screening and Missingness' and 'Qualitative Analysis and Mixed Evidence'. Merge them. Heading capitalization is also mixed (sentence case vs title case) in Chapters 4 and 6.

The disclaimer that gaze contingency, memory and Jev are shared and not tested on their own appears in the abstract, Chapter 1 (twice), Chapter 2 (four or more times), Chapters 3, 4, 6 and 8, and the conclusion. Keep it in Chapter 1's Scope section, Chapter 4's Design section and Chapter 8, and cut the rest. The same goes for the 'appealing but not faster / eerie but efficient' contrast, which recurs in Chapters 1, 2, 8 and 9.

The estimand's scale is unclear. Chapter 6 refers to a 'voice time ratio' and a 'marginal contrast standardized over the starting-difficulty distribution', but does not say whether this is a ratio of geometric means (log scale) or of arithmetic means (seconds). It also does not say why standardization changes anything when the primary model has no voice-by-theta interaction. Settle this before preregistration; I did not change the statistical specification.

The two definitions of instruction count may not match. Chapter 4 counts delivered 'guidance utterances'. Chapter 5's planned total includes gaze/pointing acknowledgments and selection reminders. State explicitly whether acknowledgments count as instructions.

The readiness lists don't match each other. The Preface and the Chapter 9 conclusion omit the unenforced left/right split, the unfrozen timeout and stopping procedure, the survey voice-reminder format, the vicinity tolerance for the study release, the multiplicity families, and the opening-cue clip-duration differences between voices. Make one list in Appendix D (readiness) and cross-reference it.

Two references depend on material not introduced in the main text. Chapter 7 mentions an 'investigation of two-second delays' and Chapter 8 mentions 'the known lower-versus-higher confusion'. Either introduce each briefly with an appendix cross-reference or remove it. I could not check the appendices.

The Yang et al. embodied-navigation paragraph sits under 'Voice as a Social and Personalized Interface' but is about presenting navigation assistance. It would fit better in the guidance or context-aware agent sections.

Pre-reveal voice exposure is not controlled. Opening cues are excluded from active time, yet their clip durations may differ between voices. Chapter 5 keeps the full opening-cue-to-selection interval but doesn't say how that interval will be reported as a possible voice-related difference.

The narrative voice is inconsistent: 'we log' (Chapter 3) and 'our adaptation' (Chapter 2) sit alongside impersonal prose. The text also leans heavily on constructions like 'rather than', 'does not establish' and 'is not X but Y'. Do a full-manuscript pass after the structural cuts.

Language edits don't make the thesis ready to submit. These substantive items are still open: the exact pre-cue theta snapshot, enforcement of the 20/20 vertical split, a simulation-based sample size, pilot acceptance criteria, reconciling consent with ElevenLabs and Jev cloud processing, the timeout and stopping rules, preregistration of multiplicity families, author and advisor front matter, final AI-disclosure approval, and Qualtrics (still on hold).

I could not check the appendices, figures, bibliography entries or the accuracy of the citations; only the main file and Chapters 1–9 were supplied. Two tables in Chapter 4 and Chapter 7 have no labels, so they cannot be cross-referenced.
